questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Normal force magnitude on a bank
questions.learningObjective: Compute the normal force on a block at rest on a frictionless banked ramp
questions.stem: Ticket 1: A 4 kg block rests on a frictionless ramp tilted 30 deg; what is the normal force magnitude?

options.text: The normal force is mg cos30 because only the perpendicular weight component presses on the ramp.
The normal force equals mg because weight fully presses on every surface.
options.misconception: treats weight as always perpendicular to the surface

options.text: The normal force is mg sin30 because the parallel component dominates contact.
options.misconception: confuses the parallel component with the normal force

options.text: The normal force is mg / cos30 because tilting increases the push.
options.misconception: inverts the cosine factor for the inclined plane

questions.explanation: On a frictionless incline at rest, vertical equilibrium gives N = mg cosθ. The tempting ideas use the full weight or invert the cosine factor.
questions.hint: Resolve weight into components perpendicular to the ramp.

questions.learningObjective: Compare banked-curve data to identify the largest normal force
questions.stem: Ticket 2: A table lists three banked curves with radius and speed; which comparison best identifies the curve with the largest normal force?

options.text: Compare only the radii; the largest radius gives the largest normal force.
options.misconception: attributes normal force to radius alone

options.text: Compare mv^2/r plus weight; the largest required centripetal term plus weight wins.
Compare only the speeds; the fastest curve has the largest normal force.
options.misconception: attributes normal force to speed alone

options.text: All three curves have the same normal force because mass is equal.
options.misconception: assumes normal force is independent of speed and radius

questions.explanation: Normal force on a banked curve reflects both weight and the centripetal requirement. Speed and radius both matter, not just one.
questions.hint: Combine the centripetal term with the weight component.

options.text: Friction is always required because gravity pulls the car inward.

options.text: Friction is required outward because the car tends to slide down.

options.text: At the design speed no friction is needed because the bank angle supplies the centripetal component.
Friction is required inward because speed exceeds the design value.
options.misconception: confuses a higher speed with the design-speed case

questions.explanation: At the design speed, the horizontal component of the normal force provides centripetal acceleration. Friction is not needed in that special case.
questions.hint: Match speed to the bank angle's centripetal component.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the error in a claim about mass and distance changes
questions.stem: Ticket 4: A code comment claims gravitational force doubles when one mass doubles and distance doubles; find the error.

questions.explanation: Doubling one mass doubles force, but doubling distance divides force by four. The net factor is one-half.

questions.stem: Ticket 43: On a frictionless banked curve at design speed, why is no friction needed?

options.text: Because speed is zero.
Because the horizontal component of normal force supplies centripetal force.
Because gravity disappears on curves.
Because friction is always zero on banks.

questions.explanation: At design speed, N sinθ = mv^2/r, so the normal force's horizontal component provides centripetal acceleration. No friction is required.
questions.hint: Resolve normal force into horizontal and vertical components.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Identify the quantities in universal gravitation
questions.stem: Ticket 44: Gravitational force between two masses depends on which quantities?

options.text: Masses and their velocities.
Distance only.
The two masses and the distance between their centers.
The masses and the medium between them.

questions.explanation: Universal gravitation depends on the two masses and their separation. Velocity and medium do not appear in the law.
questions.hint: Recall F = G m1 m2 / r^2.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Scale force from 2 m to 10 m
questions.stem: Ticket 45: A table shows force 20 N at 2 m; what force at 10 m?

options.text: 4 N because force is inversely proportional to distance.
2 N because 20 divided by 10 equals 2.
0.4 N because force divides by 50.
0.8 N because force divides by 25.

questions.explanation: Distance increases by factor 5, so force divides by 25: 20/25 = 0.8 N. Inverse-linear scaling would be wrong.
questions.hint: Square the distance factor before dividing.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Correct GM/r to GM/r^2
questions.stem: Ticket 46: A note says surface gravity is GM/R (not squared); what is wrong?

options.text: The radius must be squared in the denominator.
G should be replaced by g.
Mass should be radius.
The formula should multiply by R.

questions.explanation: Surface gravity is GM/R^2. Using GM/R gives incorrect units and overestimates gravity for small bodies.
questions.hint: Square the radius in the denominator.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Compute weight with g=1.6
questions.stem: Ticket 47: On a planet with g=1.6 m/s^2, weight of a 70 kg astronaut?
questions.explanation: Weight = mg = 70*1.6 = 112 N. The astronaut's mass stays 70 kg everywhere.
questions.hint: Multiply mass by the local g.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Compute free-fall distance in 3 seconds
questions.stem: Ticket 48: From rest, distance fallen in 3 s near Earth (g=9.8)?
questions.explanation: d = 0.5*g*t^2 = 0.5*9.8*9 = 44.1 m. Mass does not affect the distance.
questions.hint: Use d = one-half g t squared.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Describe forces between equal masses
questions.stem: Ticket 49: If two masses are equal, the gravitational forces they exert on each other are:

options.text: Equal only if distance is zero.
Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
Zero because equal masses cancel.
Determined by the larger acceleration.

questions.explanation: Equal masses are irrelevant to force equality; action-reaction always gives equal and opposite forces. Accelerations may differ only if masses differ.
questions.hint: Apply Newton's third law directly.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: State the stable circular orbit speed relation
questions.stem: Ticket 50: For a stable circular orbit, speed must satisfy which relation?

options.text: v = sqrt(GM r).
v = GM/r.
v = sqrt(GM/r).
v = G M r / v.

questions.explanation: Equating gravity to centripetal force and solving gives v = sqrt(GM/r). The radius belongs in the denominator inside the square root.
questions.hint: Solve GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r for v.

questions.learningObjective: Check a table value against mg cosθ
questions.stem: Ticket 51: Data show N=34 N for m=4 kg, θ=30°, g=9.8; is this consistent with mg cosθ?

options.text: No, because normal force equals weight 39 N.
No, because 4*9.8*sin30=19.6 N.
options.misconception: uses sine instead of cosine for normal force

options.text: Yes, because tilt does not change normal force.
Yes, because mg cos30 is about 34 N.

questions.explanation: 4*9.8*cos30 is about 33.9 N, so 34 N matches the model. The cosine factor is required.
questions.hint: Compute mg cos30 and compare.

questions.learningObjective: Identify missing factors in a normal-force report
questions.stem: Ticket 52: A report compares normal forces using radius only; what's missing?

options.text: Speed and bank angle also affect normal force.
Mass is the only missing factor.
Gravity is irrelevant to banked curves.
Radius is irrelevant; only speed matters.

questions.explanation: Normal force on a banked curve depends on speed, radius, mass, and bank angle. Radius alone is insufficient.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Compute friction force on a flat curve
questions.stem: Ticket 53: A 1200 kg car rounds a flat 60 m radius curve at 18 m/s; required friction force in newtons?
questions.explanation: Friction supplies centripetal force: 1200*18^2/60 = 6480 N. Higher speed or smaller radius would require more.
questions.hint: Use F = mv^2/r.

questions.learningObjective: Compute gravitational force for 1 kg and 4 kg
questions.stem: Ticket 54: Two masses, 1 kg and 4 kg, are 2 m apart; gravitational force using G=6.67e-11?
questions.explanation: F = 6.67e-11*1*4/2^2 = 6.67e-11 N. The numerator and denominator both use the given masses and distance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Combine mass and distance changes
questions.stem: Ticket 55: If one mass is halved and distance is halved, force changes by what factor?

options.text: One-half.
Two.
One-eighth.
Four.

questions.explanation: Halving mass halves force, but halving distance multiplies force by four. The net factor is two.
questions.hint: Combine the mass factor and squared distance factor.

questions.learningObjective: Predict g when radius doubles
questions.stem: Ticket 56: If a planet's radius doubles while mass stays same, surface gravity becomes:

options.text: Double.
Same.
One-quarter.
One-half.

questions.explanation: g = GM/R^2, so doubling R divides g by four. Mass is unchanged.
questions.hint: Square the radius change in the denominator.

questions.learningObjective: Correct the claim that free-fall time depends on mass
questions.stem: Ticket 58: A note says free-fall time depends on mass; identify the error.

options.text: Free-fall acceleration is independent of mass in vacuum.
Time depends on mass squared.
Mass affects time only for light objects.
The note is correct.

questions.explanation: In vacuum all objects have the same acceleration g, so fall time from a given height is mass-independent. Air resistance is a separate effect.
questions.hint: Remove mass from the free-fall time model.

questions.stem: Ticket 60: A satellite orbits at radius 8e6 m around Earth (M=6e24 kg); compute orbital speed using G=6.67e-11.
